title: The Target Is Not the Host: Reading a Target Triple, and the Same Struct in Four Sizes

questions.question: What does the target triple x86_64-w64-mingw32 name?
options: A compiler: the name of the program that builds for Windows
A library: the C runtime the program links against
A target: architecture, vendor and system, with the system last since the second part is not an operating system
A board: the hardware the program is flashed to
questions.explanation: A triple names what the code is built for. With three parts, if the second is not an operating system it is read as architecture, vendor and system.

questions.question: What is odd about long on 64 bit Windows?
options: It is 64 bits, as on every 64 bit machine
It is unsigned, where it is signed on Linux
It is 16 bits, kept from older versions of Windows
It is 32 bits, where it is 64 on 64 bit Linux
questions.explanation: Code that uses long for a 64 bit value breaks only there. The two Windows targets are 64 bit machines with a 32 bit long. Code that puts a 64 bit value in a long works on every Linux target and fails only there.

questions.question: The same struct was 40 bytes on x86_64, 32 on 32 bit ARM and 28 on i686. Why is i686 smaller than ARM?
options: i686 has smaller pointers than 32 bit ARM
i686 leaves out the padding at the end of the struct
32 bit ARM stores a long in 8 bytes
32 bit x86 aligns an eight byte field to 4, and 32 bit ARM to 8
questions.explanation: Both have 4 byte pointers and longs. The difference is where an 8 byte field may start, which is part of each target's rules.

questions.question: { char, int64 } holds only fixed width types. Why is it not safe to send as it is?
options: It is 16 bytes on the 64 bit targets and 12 on 32 bit x86, because of the int64's alignment
It is: fixed width types have the same layout everywhere
The char is signed on some targets and unsigned on others
It is too small for a network packet
questions.explanation: The fields are the same size everywhere, but the padding before the int64 is 7 bytes where it aligns to 8 and 3 where it aligns to 4.

questions.question: What should the parser do with a triple it cannot read?
options: Use the host's triple instead
Pick the closest known triple
Be invalid with no word sizes
Fall back to x86_64-linux-gnu, the most common
questions.explanation: A reader that guesses builds for the wrong machine without a word. Nine malformed triples all came back invalid with a pointer width of 0. A guess would build for some machine, and nothing would say it was the wrong one.

questions.question: How do you check a struct's size on the real target?
options: Print sizeof on the laptop and compare with the table
A static_assert on sizeof in the header, compiled by the cross compiler
Trust the layout model, which applies the target's rules
Ask the maker of the board
questions.explanation: The model here was never run on that machine. The model's numbers for ARM and i686 are the rules applied, not measurements. An assertion compiled by the real cross compiler fails the build if they are wrong.
